1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 71-year-old man. In June of last year, he developed dizziness and fatigue without a clear precipitating cause, with an unsteady gait while walking requiring assistance, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He was seen in the Department of Neurology at local Hospital A, where head CT indicated "subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy." After symptomatic supportive treatment, the symptoms did not improve, and beginning the next day he developed high fever with a maximum temperature of 39℃, accompanied by chills and diarrhea with watery stools. He had no nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, sputum production, chest tightness, or shortness of breath. Abdominal CT at local Hospital B showed only hepatic and renal cystic lesions and an intrahepatic calcified lesion. Complete blood count: WBC 12.22×10^9/L, N 82.3%. He was given empiric cephalosporin anti-infective therapy and symptomatic supportive treatment including antiemetic and antidiarrheal therapy for 2 days. His temperature returned to normal, but the fatigue and dizziness never improved; he was listless and unable to get out of bed to walk. In the outpatient/emergency department of our hospital, head MRI was completed and showed "multiple cerebral ischemic lesions and lacunar infarcts." Repeat complete blood count: WBC 5.6×10^9/L, N 69%; blood biochemistry showed: ALT 93U/L, albumin 25.0g/L, potassium 3.41mmol/L, sodium 129mmol/L. He was admitted to the Neurology ward of our hospital on Day 0. Past history: 2-year history of diabetes mellitus, treated with oral metformin; more than 10-year history of hypertension, highest recorded blood pressure 170/95mmHg, controlled with valsartan. Personal history: alcohol use for 40 years, drinking 1.5 jin of yellow rice wine daily, quit drinking 1 year ago; no smoking habit. Physical examination on admission: temperature 36.7℃, pulse 72 beats/min, respirations 18 breaths/min, blood pressure 130/80mmHg, clear consciousness, breathing unlabored, clear breath sounds in both lungs without dry or wet rales, heart rate 90 beats/min, regular rhythm, abdomen without tenderness, rebound tenderness, or guarding, and no edema in either lower extremity. Neurologic examination: clear consciousness. Speech fluent, appeared listless, orientation, comprehension, memory, and calculation normal. No abnormalities on cranial nerve examination. Muscle strength grade 5, normal muscle tone, tendon reflexes in all four extremities not elicited, pathologic reflexes negative, broad-based gait. Before admission, on Day -4, complete blood count showed: WBC 12.22×10^9/L↑, N 82.3%↑; upper abdominal CT: intrahepatic calcified lesion and cystic lesion, left renal cystic lesion; head CT: subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy; ECG: sinus tachycardia, frequent premature atrial contractions. On Day -2, complete blood count showed: WBC 5.6×10^9/L, N 69%, RBC 4.17×10^12/L, Hb 129g/L, CRP 3.68mg/L. Blood biochemistry: total bilirubin 13.4umol/L, albumin 25g/L↓, glucose 10.3mmol/L, potassium 3.41mmol/L↓, sodium 131mmol/L↓.

differential_diagnoses.name: Legionella infection (may present as atypical pneumonia or as a systemic infection predominantly with extrapulmonary manifestations)
supporting_evidence: Illness onset in June of last year, with high fever, maximum body temperature 39℃, accompanied by chills
Also accompanied by diarrhea with watery stools, nausea, and vomiting
Neurologic manifestations are present: dizziness, fatigue, unsteady gait, requiring assistance with ambulation
Blood biochemistry showed sodium 129-131 mmol/L↓, consistent with hyponatremia
ALT elevated to 93 U/L, suggesting abnormal liver enzymes
Pre-admission complete blood count showed WBC 12.22×10^9/L↑ and N 82.3%↑, suggesting a tendency toward acute infection
Age 71 years, with diabetes mellitus, belonging to a population susceptible to severe infection
opposing_evidence: No respiratory symptoms such as cough, sputum production, chest tightness, or shortness of breath
On admission, breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or moist rales.
In the first stage, no evidence of abnormalities on chest imaging was provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Posterior circulation ischemic stroke/cerebellar or brainstem infarction
supporting_evidence: At disease onset, there were dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and unsteady gait while walking, requiring assistance from others, consistent with common manifestations of posterior circulation involvement
Neurologic examination revealed a wide-based gait
The patient is a 71-year-old man with a history of hypertension for more than 10 years and diabetes mellitus for 2 years, both of which are risk factors for stroke.
Head MRI showed "multiple cerebral ischemic lesions and lacunar infarcts"
Head CT suggested "subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy," supporting a cerebrovascular disease background
opposing_evidence: Conscious, with normal orientation, comprehension, memory, and calculation ability
No abnormalities were found on all cranial nerve-related examinations.
Muscle strength grade 5, normal muscle tone, pathological reflexes negative, no definite focal neurologic deficits
High fever, diarrhea, and watery stools are not easily explained by cerebral infarction alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious gastroenteritis with dehydration/electrolyte disturbance
supporting_evidence: Developed high fever, with a maximum temperature of 39℃, accompanied by chills
Accompanied by diarrhea, passing watery stools, with nausea and vomiting
Before admission, complete blood count showed WBC 12.22×10^9/L ↑ and N 82.3% ↑, supporting acute infection.
After fluid replacement and empiric anti-infective treatment with cephalosporins, body temperature returned to normal
Hyponatremia (129-131 mmol/L) and hypokalemia (3.41 mmol/L) are present, which may be related to diarrhea/vomiting.
Marked fatigue, unable to get out of bed and walk, which may be exacerbated by post-infectious dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
opposing_evidence: Abdominal examination showed no tenderness, rebound tenderness, or guarding.
Abdominal CT showed only cystic lesions in the liver and kidneys and intrahepatic calcified lesions, with no definite evidence of an acute abdomen.
After body temperature returned to normal, fatigue, dizziness, and unsteady gait persisted, suggesting that they cannot be fully explained by simple gastroenteritis alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hyponatremia-related metabolic encephalopathy / symptomatic electrolyte disturbance
supporting_evidence: Serum sodium 129-131 mmol/L ↓
Accompanied by fatigue, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and unsteady gait
Concomitant hypokalemia (3.41 mmol/L↓) and hypoalbuminemia (25 g/L↓) were present, suggesting internal milieu disturbance and poor nutritional status.
Diarrhea and watery stool may cause or exacerbate hyponatremia
The neurologic examination lacks definite focal localizing signs, which is more supportive of involvement of metabolic/systemic factors.
opposing_evidence: The degree of hyponatremia was mild to moderate, with no severe manifestations of hyponatremia such as seizures or obvious disturbance of consciousness.
Fever and elevated neutrophils are present, suggesting a possible concomitant infectious etiology.

differential_diagnoses.name: Wernicke encephalopathy or alcohol-related nutritional deficiency encephalopathy
supporting_evidence: Has a 40-year history of alcohol use, drinks 1.5 jin of yellow rice wine daily, suggesting a history of long-term alcohol exposure
Unsteady gait/wide-based gait
Accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and lethargy
Albumin 25 g/L↓, suggesting poor nutritional status or chronic wasting
opposing_evidence: Cranial nerve-related examinations were all normal, with no description of abnormal eye movements or ophthalmoplegia.
Conscious, with normal orientation, comprehension, memory, and calculation; no obvious disturbance of consciousness or cognitive impairment.
The patient quit drinking 1 year ago
High fever, diarrhea, and elevated neutrophils are not consistent with the typical manifestations of pure Wernicke encephalopathy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome (postinfectious peripheral neuropathy)
supporting_evidence: Diarrhea before and after disease onset, with watery stools, which may serve as a preceding event of post-infectious immune-mediated neuropathy
Unable to get out of bed to walk; markedly unsteady gait
Deep tendon reflexes in all four extremities could not be elicited, suggesting possible peripheral nerve involvement
opposing_evidence: Muscle strength grade 5; no progressive symmetric limb weakness observed
No sensory abnormality described
No dyspnea, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, breathing unlabored
High fever and an elevated neutrophil count are more suggestive of an acute infectious process and cannot be explained by Guillain-Barré syndrome alone.

stage2_input.text: After admission, on Day +1, complete blood count showed: WBC 6.5x10^9/L, N 68.7%, Hb 135g/L, Plt 200×10^9/L. CRP 270.30mg/L↑. PCT 0.475ng/ml. IL6 149.4pg/mL↑. Blood culture: no bacterial growth; bacterial endotoxin <5pg/ml, fungal D-glucan test <31.25pg/ml. Routine biochemistry: alanine aminotransferase: 146U/L↑, aspartate aminotransferase: 173U/L↑, glucose: 9.9mmol/L, uric acid: 114umol/L, sodium: 126mmol/L↓, chloride: 92mmol/L, calcium: 2.05mmol/L, phosphorus: 0.38mmol/L. Coagulation studies: INR 1.21, PT activity 69.9%, activated partial thromboplastin time 42.3S, fibrinogen 8.67g/L, D-dimer 2.17ug/ml, FDP: 11.4mg/L. Tumor markers/immunology: NSE: 33.8ug/L↑, CA125: 44.61U/ml↑; CEA, CYFRA211, AFP, CA199, and SCC were all normal. Lumbar puncture, routine cerebrospinal fluid studies, biochemistry, and other tests showed no abnormalities. The patient suddenly developed high fever again, with temperature rising to 40℃. Chest radiograph was completed, showing patchy linear high-density opacity in the left mid-lung field and blunting of the left costophrenic angle. Chest CT showed bilateral lung inflammation, predominantly on the left, a small left pleural effusion, with localized atelectasis, and a small pericardial effusion. Routine repeat liver function testing showed ALT increased to 154U/L, significantly higher than previously. During hospitalization, the patient again developed fever, with marked fatigue and inability to stand, and again developed dizziness and nausea. Repeat chest CT (Day +1, Day +13) showed progression compared with prior of bilateral lung inflammation and bilateral pleural effusions.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Blood test on Day +16: fungal (1,3)-β-D-glucan test 390 pg/ml ↑
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 71-year-old elderly male with diabetes mellitus. During hospitalization, he had recurrent high fever. Chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary inflammation and progressively worsening pleural effusion, and his condition remained recurrent after conventional anti-infective therapy, placing him in a susceptible population for invasive fungal infection that warrants focused evaluation. D-glucan had previously been normal and subsequently increased to 390 pg/ml, indicating that dynamic assessment is needed during the disease course to determine whether fungus-related infection has developed. This test is mainly used to screen for the possibility of invasive fungal infection, help explain persistent fever and progression of pulmonary lesions, and provide a basis for whether further bronchoscopic sampling, fungal culture, and consideration of adjustment of the anti-infective strategy are needed; at the same time, it should be interpreted together with subsequent GM testing, Cryptococcus testing, and BALF results to avoid misjudging a single elevated serologic result as the final causative etiology.

The patient has recurrent high fever, persistent progression of pulmonary inflammation, pleural effusion, underlying diabetes mellitus, and unstable response to anti-infective therapy; clinically, invasive fungal pneumonia such as invasive aspergillosis must be included in the differential diagnosis. Although elevated D-glucan suggests the possibility of a fungal-related process, its specificity is limited; therefore, a galactomannan assay is needed to further determine whether Aspergillus infection is present. This test helps address the clinical question of whether the elevated D-glucan is caused by invasive fungi such as Aspergillus; if negative, it can reduce the diagnostic likelihood of Aspergillus pneumonia, avoid unnecessary anti-Aspergillus treatment, and prompt further investigation for other pathogens such as Chlamydia, bacteria, or noninfectious causes.

The patient was of advanced age, had diabetes, and recurrent fever, and initially presented with nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, gait instability, nausea, and vomiting. Pulmonary inflammation and pleural effusion were subsequently identified. Clinically, it was necessary to rule out fungal infections such as cryptococcosis that can involve the lungs and be accompanied by systemic symptoms. Especially in the setting of elevated D-glucan, further cryptococcal latex agglutination testing helps narrow the spectrum of fungal infection. This test is mainly used to exclude cryptococcal infection as an important differential diagnosis, avoiding misattribution of the pulmonary lesions and systemic symptoms to cryptococcosis, which could affect subsequent anti-infective regimen selection; a negative result also helps shift the diagnostic focus to other pathogens.

The patient's disease course was prolonged. During hospitalization, there were multiple episodes of high fever, and imaging showed persistent progression of bilateral pulmonary inflammation and pleural effusion, suggesting an ongoing inflammatory or infectious process in the body. Although ESR lacks specificity, it has some value in assessing the activity of chronic or subacute inflammation and in assisting the differentiation of infection from other inflammatory diseases. The clinical purpose of this test is to assess disease severity from the perspective of overall inflammatory burden and, together with CRP, pleural fluid results, and etiologic test results, to determine whether there is TB, fungal infection, tumor, or organizing pneumonia and other protracted diseases; an elevated result supports the presence of a significant inflammatory response in the body, indicating the need for continued in-depth investigation of the cause rather than management solely as ordinary community-acquired pneumonia.

The patient had recurrent fever, progression of pulmonary lesions despite treatment, and pleural effusion with lymphocyte-predominant pleural fluid; these features make TB infection one of the differential diagnoses that must be excluded. In particular, pulmonary TB in elderly patients may present atypically, with imaging overlap with common pneumonia, tumor, or other chronic infections. This test was performed primarily to answer the key question of whether TB infection was present, to help explain the source of the pulmonary inflammation and pleural effusion, and to affect isolation measures and anti-TB treatment decisions. Combined with negative T-cell testing, pleural fluid ADA not elevated, and subsequent pathogen results, the likelihood of TB can be reduced and inappropriate treatment minimized.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Pleural fluid routine analysis: appearance, yellow and slightly turbid; specific gravity, not measured due to insufficient volume; Rivalta test, weakly positive; red blood cell count, 4000x10^6/L; white blood cell count, 2805x10^6/L; segmented neutrophils, 3%; lymphocytes, 89%; monocytes, 8%
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Chest CT showed pleural effusion, and repeat examination indicated progression of bilateral pleural effusions, accompanied by recurrent high fever and persistent pulmonary inflammation; therefore, direct evaluation of the nature of the pleural fluid is very important. Routine pleural fluid analysis can preliminarily determine whether the effusion is exudative or transudative and can suggest the type of infection through differential cell count analysis. This test is mainly intended to determine whether the pleural effusion is a simple parapneumonic effusion, tuberculous pleurisy, tumor-related effusion, or caused by other reasons. The results showed yellow, slightly turbid fluid, Rivalta weakly positive, elevated white blood cells, and a high lymphocyte proportion, which helps suggest an exudative effusion and supports further pleural fluid biochemistry, TB, and etiologic differentiation, while also providing direction for the subsequent diagnostic pathway.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Pleural fluid biochemistry: total protein 42.1 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 198 U/L, adenosine deaminase 20 U/L
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: With the patient’s pleural effusion persistently present and progressing, imaging alone cannot determine the cause of the effusion, and further assessment must be made in conjunction with pleural fluid biochemistry. During the course of illness, the patient had recurrent high fever and persistent pulmonary lesions, and clinically differentiation is needed from tuberculous pleuritis, bacterial pleural infection, and malignant pleural effusion. The purpose of this test is to determine the exudative nature based on total protein and LDH, to assess the possibility of TB using ADA, and to help analyze whether complicated infectious pleural effusion is present. In the results, elevated total protein supports exudative pleural effusion, and ADA 20U/L does not support tuberculous pleuritis, which is important for excluding TB, narrowing the differential diagnosis, and shifting attention to other pathogen-related pneumonia, especially atypical pathogens.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was completed for pathogen testing; no abnormalities were seen in the bronchi at any level.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the patient mainly presented with fever and systemic symptoms and respiratory symptoms were not prominent, chest CT had already confirmed bilateral pulmonary inflammation, atelectasis, and pleural effusion, and recurrent high fever persisted despite routine empiric anti-infective therapy, suggesting that the etiology would be difficult to determine based solely on upper respiratory tract or sputum specimens. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy can directly assess whether the airways have tumor, tuberculous changes, purulent secretions, or obstructive lesions, and can obtain high-quality lower respiratory tract specimens. The main purpose of this examination is to determine the true cause of progression of the pulmonary lesions, exclude an endobronchial mass, TB, or other structural lesions, and provide a prerequisite for subsequent BALF pathogen testing; if bronchoscopy shows no abnormalities, this also helps reduce the likelihood of a central tumor or obvious endobronchial TB.

recommended_exams.exam: Pathogen testing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was completed for etiologic testing
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The greatest clinical challenge in this case was that the patient had recurrent high fever, the white blood cell count was not persistently elevated, pulmonary imaging showed progression, and conventional empiric treatment had limited efficacy, suggesting the presence of atypical pathogens, mixed infection, or an infection not readily detected by routine culture. Pathogen testing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid can obtain specimens directly from the lower respiratory tract lesion site, with less contamination than sputum specimens and higher positive diagnostic yield. This test was intended to identify the true pathogen causing pneumonia and persistent fever and to distinguish among bacteria, fungi, TB, atypical pathogens, and even mixed infection, thereby guiding precise antimicrobial therapy; it played a key role in the final identification of Chlamydia psittaci in this case and in assessing the pathogenicity of other concomitantly detected organisms.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Fungal culture of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and metagenomic sequencing suggested infection with Candida albicans, Streptococcus mitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Chlamydia psittaci.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s underlying diabetes, elevated D-glucan, progression of pulmonary lesions, and recurrent high fever once made fungal infection an important differential diagnosis. Serology alone cannot determine whether there is truly a pathogenic fungus in the lungs, so fungal culture of BALF was needed. This test is mainly used to confirm whether fungal colonization or infection is present in the lower respiratory tract and to provide a basis for whether subsequent antifungal therapy is necessary. Although Candida albicans was detected on culture, this should be interpreted in conjunction with imaging findings that were not typical of fungal infection, negative GM and cryptococcal results, and the rapid effectiveness of subsequent doxycycline treatment, suggesting that it was more likely colonization or a non-primary pathogen. In other words, this test was critical for ruling out fungal infection as the current main cause.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Fungal culture of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and metagenomic sequencing suggested infection with Candida albicans, Streptococcus mitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Chlamydia psittaci.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's clinical presentation was highly atypical: onset with systemic symptoms such as fever, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, and unsteady gait, with no obvious respiratory symptoms early on; bilateral pulmonary inflammation and pleural effusion were not identified until chest CT after hospitalization, and the lesions continued to progress despite conventional anti-infective therapy. At this point, routine cultures and common serologic tests could not comprehensively cover atypical pathogens, especially difficult-to-culture organisms such as Chlamydia psittaci. The core value of metagenomic sequencing lies in its unbiased broad-spectrum detection of bacteria, fungi, atypical pathogens, and clues to mixed infection, thereby addressing the key question of "which pathogen is the true causative agent." Combined with the patient's epidemiologic exposure as a landscaper with frequent contact with bird feathers and droppings, as well as the rapid normalization of body temperature, symptom relief, and absorption on chest CT after doxycycline treatment, mNGS detection of Chlamydia psittaci played a decisive role in confirming the diagnosis and guiding targeted therapy, while also helping differentiate other concurrently detected microorganisms as more likely accompanying colonizers or secondary pathogens.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Blood tests on Day +16: fungal (1,3)-beta-D-glucan assay 390 pg/ml↑, galactomannan test negative; cryptococcal latex agglutination test negative; ESR 75 mm/h↑; TB infection T-cell test negative. Pleural fluid routine analysis: appearance yellow, slightly turbid; specific gravity too მცირე to measure, Rivalta test weakly positive, red blood cell count 4000x10^6/L, white blood cell count 2805x10^6/L, segmented neutrophils 3%, lymphocytes 89%, monocytes 8%; pleural fluid biochemistry: total protein 42.1 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 198 U/L, adenosine deaminase 20 U/L. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was completed for pathogen testing, and no abnormalities were seen in the bronchi at all levels. Fungal culture and metagenomic sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid suggested infection with Candida albicans, Streptococcus mitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Chlamydia psittaci. Further inquiry into the patient's occupation revealed that the patient is a landscaper whose main work is pruning flowers, plants, and trees, with indirect exposure to bird feathers, secretions, and excreta such as feces, and with frequent opportunities for such exposure.

diagnostic_basis: BALF metagenomic sequencing indicated Chlamydia psittaci.
The patient is a landscaper whose main work is pruning flowers, plants, and trees, with frequent indirect exposure to bird feathers, secretions, and excreta such as droppings.
The patient's clinical symptoms were predominantly fever, with no expectoration; fever persisted after the white blood cell count returned to normal on the complete blood count.

Exclude Candida albicans: although the patient has diabetes mellitus, the chest CT findings are not typical imaging findings of fungal infection, and the body temperature temporarily returned to normal after antibiotic treatment

Streptococcus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were excluded: the ceftazidime, levofloxacin, and others used have already covered the corresponding pathogens, treatment was temporarily effective, and they are not the main causative pathogens at the current stage.
Tuberculosis infection excluded: based on relevant tests such as TSPOT and pleural fluid adenosine deaminase, the possibility of tuberculosis infection was excluded

treatment_response: Beginning the next day, the patient's body temperature rapidly returned to normal, and symptoms such as dizziness and fatigue were relieved.
After 2 weeks of doxycycline treatment, the patient no longer had fever and had no dizziness, fatigue, vomiting, or other symptoms; the general condition was good.
Repeat chest CT: pneumonia has been significantly absorbed compared with previously.
